Simulacra
A horror game that thrives on its concept: digging through a stranger’s phone to uncover dark secrets. It manages to feel unsettling in a very modern and realistic way, and the mystery at the core is engaging enough to keep you scrolling and piecing together clues.

That said, the game often stumbles when it comes to presentation. The acting is inconsistent, and the dialogue can feel awkward or unintentional funny, which breaks the immersion during otherwise tense moments.

Even with its flaws, it’s an experience that sticks with you — unique, creepy, and worth checking out if you’re looking for something different in the horror genre. 
7.5/10

The first run was easily one of the best horror games I have played thus far. The dialogue choices aren't as painful as other game's options that I have played before, and some of the jumpscares are genuinely decent. The text scramble and picture debugging games are generally quick and easy to do while not being too easy that it's boring. 
However, after the first run, all of the horror is sucked out of it. All the diverging paths are at the very end and it's difficult to get some of the endings. I can give credit for the concept of the antagonist being the software itself, though its motives are exactly like pretty much every other humanity eradicating AI on the internet. 
The theme music is an absolute banger, though.

I picked up this game for less than a pack of gums, and it's phenomenal for the price you pay for it. It reminded me of [i] Her Story, [/i] another indie game that was released 2 years before this, so if you liked that, you'll like this as well. It is also similar to [i] Life is Strange, Until Dawn, the Telltale games, Deus Ex Human Revolution, [/i] but this is much lighter and made by a smaller team. 

Unlike the games mentioned earlier, your choices actually matter. If you go in thinking "oh I'm going to play this game and I'll get the good ending and I'll be done with it", then you're wrong. It doesn't work like that, and you can screw up your ending very early on. If [i] Until Dawn [/i] let you save the characters you want by using common sense, Simulacra is not as forgiving. Even if you try to reason with the characters like in [i] Deus Ex, [/i] that's not always going to work. The overall story is entertaining and the characters are great, however, there are some typos, the voice calls are cheesy because they're overdone, being shot in a studio, and the game tries to scare you with its ambience sounds, which aren't connected to the story in any way. There are also some puzzles, some easier, others are harder, which make the game more enjoyable as it's not that linear and actually puts up a challenge.

Overall, I found the game enjoyable. It's replayable, the choices that you make actually have some sort of impact, and the characters are great. There's also a Simulacra spin-off that is free, and there are some sequels. If you didn't get the ending that you wished for, don't feel bad. Some endings are easier to get than others.

[b]Simulacra[/b] is a "found phone" game—a genre where players uncover clues after discovering a stranger's lost smartphone. While the concept has gained popularity in the last decade, games have experimented with faux interfaces mimicking imagined technology for years. I remember playing Mean Streets and the officially licensed X-Files game, both of which attempted something similar.

In Simulacra, you navigate the protagonist's phone within the game's tightly controlled framework, piecing together what happened to its owner. I was initially drawn to the game due to the resurgence of modern full-motion video (FMV) storytelling. Having enjoyed 2015's Her Story, I expected a similar experience. While Simulacra integrates FMV clips effectively, its "found phone" premise was far less compelling to me. I think I hit an audience mismatch—I’m simply not a fan of smartphones. Since I don't particularly enjoy using my own phone, the idea of rifling through someone else’s was unappealing. I played on my laptop and embarrassingly took about a third of the game to realize that it was undoubtedly designed to be played on a smartphone—duh.

The protagonist, Anna, feels like a generic twenty-something woman struggling with rocky relationships, an unfulfilling job, and repeated rejections in her academic and professional pursuits. [spoiler]She has a non-binary best friend, which the game seemingly frames as a revelation, but it’s so heavily telegraphed that it falls into cliché territory.[/spoiler] In fact, Anna herself is a walking cliché, as is the familiar "technology is evil" theme—an overused trope in uninspired sci-fi narratives. After seeing it so often, it no longer has much impact for me.

The game’s title did surprise me. Before playing, I had never encountered the terms "Simulacra" or "Simulacrum," which piqued my curiosity. Midway through, I looked up the meaning, wondering why a game about a woman's lost phone would have such a name. Ah, crap—spoilers.

As for gameplay, Simulacra offers little freedom. Players must follow rigidly scripted conversations in a precise order to unlock new options and clues. While there are minor choices in how you interact with Anna’s close friends, they ultimately boil down to a few dialogue changes that determine which of the five endings you get—most of which depend on choices made in the last 10% of the game. That said, I appreciated that I could make all the necessary connections without resorting to a guide or hints. That sense of progress and accomplishment is something lacking in other puzzle or adventure games.

Overall, Simulacra is predictable but not necessarily bad. The FMV clips are well-integrated, Wendy Van Horen Carneiro delivers a solid performance as the wronged damsel in distress, and the faux-phone interface is thoughtfully designed. I give it a [b]3 out of 5[/b]—though the game is clearly aimed at a different audience than me, so others may find it more engaging.
